lessons.title: Angles and exact trigonometric values
lessons.summary: Use the unit circle to find the value and sign of sine, cosine and tangent in degrees or radians.
lessons.objective: Use the unit circle to find the value and sign of sine, cosine and tangent in degrees or radians.
lessons.before: Use this lesson to use the unit circle to find the value and sign of sine, cosine and tangent in degrees or radians.
lessons.ideas:
Start from the positive horizontal axis. The point reached on a unit circle is \((\cos x,\sin x)\).

A reference angle is the small positive angle between the final direction and the horizontal axis. Use the special triangles for \(30^\circ,45^\circ,60^\circ\).

A half-turn can be named \(180^\circ\) or \(\pi\) radians. The rotation and trig value are unchanged.
lessons.method:
Imagine a stick of length one rotating about the origin. Looking at its tip, read the signed horizontal position first and the signed vertical position second. The horizontal entry gives cosine and the vertical entry gives sine. Angles drawn anticlockwise are positive. Angles drawn clockwise are negative. Add or subtract \(360^\circ\) to bring an angle to a familiar direction without moving its final point.

For \(45^\circ\), equal legs and Pythagoras give a hypotenuse \(\sqrt2\) times a leg. For \(30^\circ\) and \(60^\circ\), split an equilateral triangle in half. The short leg, long leg and hypotenuse have ratio \(1:\sqrt3:2\). The triangle supplies the size. Read the sign from the actual quadrant. With a point on an axis, read its coordinates from the circle instead of drawing a triangle.

Check the unit stated in the question before entering an angle on a calculator. To move from degrees to radians, multiply by pi and divide by 180. To move back, reverse the conversion. Keep a radian answer in terms of pi when the question asks for exact values. The same quadrants and signs still apply. A negative angle can also be moved forward by whole turns.
mistakes: Both legs of an ordinary triangle have positive lengths. Coordinates in other quadrants can be negative, so the trig values can also be negative.
The tangent is the quotient \(\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}\). Avoid reversing the ratio.
An angle measured in radians does not carry the degree symbol. In a mixed comparison, convert both angles before deciding which is larger.

examples.title: Read an exact trigonometric value
examples.question: Find the exact value of \(\sin\left(\frac{2 \pi}{3}\right)\).
examples.solution:
After removing whole turns, evaluate \(\sin\left(\frac{2 \pi}{3}\right)\).

The reference angle is \(\frac{\pi}{3}\). Use the signs of the coordinates in the actual quadrant.

Sine has exact value \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

Answer: \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

examples.title: Read an exact trigonometric value
examples.question: Find the exact value of \(\tan\left(- \frac{2 \pi}{3}\right)\).
examples.solution:
After removing whole turns, evaluate \(\tan\left(\frac{4 \pi}{3}\right)\).

The reference angle is \(\frac{\pi}{3}\). Use the signs of the coordinates in the actual quadrant.

Tangent has exact value \(\sqrt{3}\).

Answer: \(\sqrt{3}\).

examples.title: Switch angle units
examples.question: Convert \(210^\circ\) to radians as a multiple of \(\pi\).
examples.solution:
A half-turn is both \(180^\circ\) and \(\pi\) radians.

Multiply by \(\frac{\pi}{180}\) and simplify.

Answer: \(\frac{7 \pi}{6}\).

lessons.title: Basic graphs and periodicity
lessons.summary: Draw and read sine, cosine and tangent, including their zeros, repeats and differences.
lessons.objective: Draw and read sine, cosine and tangent, including their zeros, repeats and differences.
lessons.before: Use this lesson to draw and read sine, cosine and tangent, including their zeros, repeats and differences.
lessons.ideas:
Mark the values at quarter turns first. The sine graph starts at zero and the cosine graph starts at its maximum.

The period is the smallest positive horizontal distance that gives the same complete shape again.

Tangent is \(\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}\). The curve is undefined where cosine is zero and repeats every half-turn.
lessons.method:
Draw a horizontal angle axis and a vertical value axis. Use evenly spaced quarter-turn marks. Follow the unit-circle coordinates through one turn to plot the first curve. For sine, the coordinate goes up, back to zero, down and back to zero. For cosine, the coordinate starts at the right-hand edge of the circle, which gives its maximum. Join the plotted points with a smooth curve and use a ruler for the axes.

Choose matching points facing the same direction. Two successive rising zeros of sine are one whole cycle apart. A rising zero and the next falling zero are separated by only half a cycle. In a formula with a scaled angle, start from the basic period and divide by the angle multiplier.

FunctionFull period in degreesFull period in radians
Sine or cosine\(360^\circ\)\(2\pi\)
Tangent\(180^\circ\)\(\pi\)

Use the denominator to find an asymptote. Draw a dashed vertical line there before sketching the curve. Between two asymptotes, tangent runs through all real values. Through its zeros the curve rises, on both sides of a quarter-turn it approaches different ends of the y-axis, and across the asymptote it breaks. For sine and cosine a scale changes the height, but for tangent there is no greatest or least y-value.
mistakes: A sine graph starting at its maximum has the cosine starting point. Read the name before drawing.
Two identical y-values can lie on different parts of the same cycle. Check the local direction or a matching peak.
Do not join tangent across an asymptote. The angle there has no value of tangent.

examples.title: Read a point on a basic graph
examples.question: The graph is \(y=\sin\left(x\right)\). Find its exact ordinate at \(x=- \frac{2 \pi}{3}\).
examples.solution:
Move along the horizontal axis to the given angle. The repeat distance is \(2 \pi\).

Reducing the input to one cycle gives the ordinate \(- \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

Answer: \(- \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

examples.title: Find the horizontal period
examples.question: Find the period of the graph \(y=8\tan\left(\frac{3}{4}x\right)+1\) in degrees.
examples.solution:
One full repeat of tangent takes \(180^\circ\) in the argument.

The input multiplier is \(\frac{3}{4}\). Divide the original period by \(\frac{3}{4}\).

Answer: \(240^\circ\).

examples.title: Label the vertical asymptotes
examples.question: Give the x-coordinates of all vertical asymptotes of \(y=6\tan\left(3x\right)+3\) for \(-60^\circ\le x\le 90^\circ\).
examples.solution:
The graph is undefined where the cosine of the argument is zero.

Within a full period, the argument is \(90^\circ\). Repeat by adding or subtracting \(180^\circ\).

The given interval for the full argument \(u=3x\) is \(-180^\circ\le u\le270^\circ\). Solve for \(x\) after listing the possible arguments.

Answer: \(x=-30^\circ,\quad 30^\circ,\quad 90^\circ\).

lessons.title: Transforming sine and cosine graphs
lessons.summary: Sketch a scaled and shifted wave, read its range and recover amplitude, midline and period.
lessons.objective: Sketch a scaled and shifted wave, read its range and recover amplitude, midline and period.
lessons.before: Use this lesson to sketch a scaled and shifted wave, read its range and recover amplitude, midline and period.
lessons.ideas:
For \(y=a\sin(bx)+c\) with positive \(a\), the extrema are \(c-a\) and \(c+a\). The cosine version follows the same rule.

The inside multiplier \(b\) controls the horizontal scale. A complete sine or cosine cycle takes \(\frac{360^\circ}{b}\) or \(\frac{2\pi}{b}\) for positive \(b\).

Read the height, centre and one full period independently. Check the starting point to choose sine or cosine.
lessons.method:
Put a dotted line at y equal to the vertical shift. This is the centre of the wave. The amplitude is the step from the centre to a peak or a trough. If the maximum and minimum are given instead, their mean gives the midline and half their difference gives the amplitude. This also tells you how to find a missing vertical scale from a graph.

Use the expression inside the brackets for the angles on the usual wave. Solve a short equation for the x-coordinate of each point. For a sketch, begin with the ends of one cycle and divide that distance into four equal parts. Scale the ordinate and apply the vertical shift. If the domain ends in the middle of a cycle, sketch only the part requested.

If the midline is \(c\) and the amplitude is \(a\), then the vertical scale and the shift are already known. Read the horizontal distance between matching peaks. Divide the standard period by this distance to find the argument multiplier. To choose a starting curve, look at the value at the origin and the direction it is moving. Check a second landmark after writing the function.
mistakes: The amplitude is half the full vertical height. The highest y-value also includes the midline shift.
An inside multiplier greater than one makes the wave reach the usual argument sooner. Divide the old period by \(b\).
An origin on the midline and heading upwards suggests sine. An origin at the maximum suggests cosine. Moving the graph vertically can hide both clues if you compare with zero instead of the centre.

examples.title: Read a maximum from the midline
examples.question: Find the maximum value of \(y=2\cos\left(\frac{1}{3}x\right)+4\).
examples.solution:
The midline is \(y=4\). The amplitude is \(2\).

The maximum is \(4+2=6\).

Answer: \(6\).

examples.title: Find the horizontal period
examples.question: Find the period of the graph \(y=7\sin\left(2x\right)-5\) in radians.
examples.solution:
One full repeat of sine takes \(2 \pi\) in the argument.

The input multiplier is \(2\). Divide the original period by \(2\).

Answer: \(\pi\).

examples.title: Recover the centre line of a wave
examples.question: A sine curve has peaks of \(1\) and troughs of \(-9\). Find the value of its midline.
examples.solution:
The line lies halfway between \(-9\) and \(1\).

Average the two values to obtain \(-4\).

Answer: \(-4\).

lessons.title: Tangent transformations and modulus graphs
lessons.summary: Label the asymptotes of a transformed tangent graph and reflect the negative parts of a trig curve.
lessons.objective: Label the asymptotes of a transformed tangent graph and reflect the negative parts of a trig curve.
lessons.before: Use this lesson to label the asymptotes of a transformed tangent graph and reflect the negative parts of a trig curve.
lessons.ideas:
The transformed tangent is undefined when the argument has zero cosine. For \(y=a\tan(bx)+c\), solve \(bx=90^\circ+180^\circ k\) in degrees.

For \(y=|f(x)|\), keep the parts at or above the horizontal axis and reflect the negative parts in that axis.

The reflected graph has no negative ordinates. Its minima occur at zero crossings or at whichever reflected part comes closest to the axis.
lessons.method:
Find the x-positions of the vertical lines before drawing a branch. A vertical shift lifts the zero of the unshifted tangent to the new midline. Use the centre crossing on either side of the vertical line as a guide. If a branch runs off the given plot, leave it open in the right direction. In radian work, start the list of arguments at pi over two and repeat by pi.

Draw a light sketch of the underlying signed curve first. Label the zeros, since these are the places where a reflected section joins an unchanged section. At a negative point, use its original x-coordinate and replace the y-value with the corresponding positive value. This process also works branch by branch for a tangent curve. An excluded x-value still has no point.

Compare the absolute values of the original extrema when the function is bounded. If the curve reaches the axis, that gives the minimum of the modulus. For sine or cosine with a shift, a half-turn does not usually repeat the reflected shape, because the peaks of the original wave were different distances from the axis. For unshifted sine or cosine it does repeat after half of the original period.
mistakes: A vertical shift does not move an asymptote left or right. Only the horizontal scale in this family changes its position.
A modulus on the outside treats the whole y-value. Reflect after applying the vertical shift, even if that changes which parts cross the axis.
A symmetry of the unshifted modulus graph does not necessarily survive a vertical shift placed inside the modulus.

examples.title: Label the vertical asymptotes
examples.question: Give the x-coordinates of all vertical asymptotes of \(y=8\tan\left(x\right)-3\) for \(-360^\circ\le x\le 180^\circ\).
examples.solution:
The graph is undefined where the cosine of the argument is zero.

Within a full period, the argument is \(90^\circ\). Repeat by adding or subtracting \(180^\circ\).

The given interval for the full argument \(u=x\) is \(-360^\circ\le u\le180^\circ\). Solve for \(x\) after listing the possible arguments.

Answer: \(x=-270^\circ,\quad -90^\circ,\quad 90^\circ\).

examples.title: Reflect a negative ordinate
examples.question: Find the exact value of \(\left|6\cos\left(\frac{1}{3}x\right)\right|\) when \(x=2610^\circ\).
examples.solution:
The unreflected argument is \(870^\circ\). This gives an ordinate of \(- 3 \sqrt{3}\).

A modulus keeps a non-negative ordinate and makes a negative ordinate positive.

Answer: \(3 \sqrt{3}\).

examples.title: Reflect a negative ordinate
examples.question: Find the exact value of \(\left|4\sin\left(2x\right)-2\right|\) when \(x=\frac{11 \pi}{4}\).
examples.solution:
The unreflected argument is \(\frac{11 \pi}{2}\). This gives an ordinate of \(-6\).

A modulus keeps a non-negative ordinate and makes a negative ordinate positive.

Answer: \(6\).

lessons.title: Solving trigonometric equations on an interval
lessons.summary: Find all special and non-special angle solutions in written bounds, including transformed arguments.
lessons.objective: Find all special and non-special angle solutions in written bounds, including transformed arguments.
lessons.before: Use this lesson to find all special and non-special angle solutions in written bounds, including transformed arguments.
lessons.ideas:
If an equation says \(\cos x=\frac12\), draw a cosine graph and a horizontal line at that level. Their intersections show all answers in the pictured interval.

In an equation such as \(\tan(2x+30^\circ)=1\), the expression \(2x+30^\circ\) is the angle the tangent sees.

For a non-special angle, keep the calculator value through all changes of period and scale. Round the final angle only when asked.
lessons.method:
Isolate the trig function first. Look up a known exact value or use an inverse function to find one principal value. The graph and circle give the other crossing in one cycle. For sine, equal ordinates reflect about the vertical diameter. For cosine, equal abscissae reflect about the horizontal diameter. Tangent needs one base angle and all its half-turn repeats.

Name the whole bracket. Multiply the original bounds by the same scale as the variable and then add the shift. Work with this new interval while listing angles. Only then undo the shift and undo the multiplication. Check an endpoint separately when it makes the equation true. A strict upper bound omits that angle. An inclusive upper bound keeps it.

Check degree or radian mode. Choose the base angle and do the reflection on the unrounded value. Sweep the full interval before rounding. Round all requested answers to the same precision. If the problem requests an exact value, leave standard angles in degrees or multiples of pi.
mistakes: The calculator returns one principal angle. A question asking for all solutions needs every compatible crossing in the stated interval.
When you double the argument, the argument interval also changes. Leaving the old bounds can hide other solutions.
Do not round a value near a boundary before testing if it belongs in the interval.

examples.title: Find every solution in the domain
examples.question: Solve \(6\sin\left(\frac{1}{2}x+30^\circ\right)+2=-1\) for \(-90^\circ\le x< 630^\circ\). Give exact answers.
examples.solution:
Subtract the constant and divide by the coefficient to obtain \(\sin\left(u\right)=- \frac{1}{2}\).

The given interval for the full argument \(u=\frac{1}{2}x+30^\circ\) is \(-15^\circ\le u<345^\circ\). Solve for \(x\) after listing the possible arguments.

Within a full period, the argument is \(210^\circ,\ 330^\circ\). Repeat by adding or subtracting \(360^\circ\).

Answer: \(x=360^\circ,\quad 600^\circ\).

examples.title: Find every solution in the domain
examples.question: Solve \(6\tan\left(x\right)+2=2 + 6 \sqrt{3}\) for \(- \frac{\pi}{2}\le x\le \frac{5 \pi}{2}\). Give exact answers.
examples.solution:
Subtract the constant and divide by the coefficient to obtain \(\tan\left(u\right)=\sqrt{3}\).

The given interval for the full argument \(u=x\) is \(- \frac{\pi}{2}\le u\le\frac{5 \pi}{2}\). Solve for \(x\) after listing the possible arguments.

Within a full period, the argument is \(\frac{\pi}{3}\). Repeat by adding or subtracting \(\pi\).

Answer: \(x=\frac{\pi}{3},\quad \frac{4 \pi}{3},\quad \frac{7 \pi}{3}\).

examples.title: Use a calculator for a non-special angle
examples.question: Solve \(\tan x=\frac{194}{133}\) for \(0\le x< 360^\circ\). Give answers to one decimal place.
examples.solution:
In degree mode, inverse tangent gives the first argument \(55.5668^\circ\).

Use the repeat distance \(180^\circ\) to find the other possible arguments before rounding.

Answer: \(x=55.6^\circ,\ 235.6^\circ\).

lessons.title: Reciprocal functions and identities
lessons.summary: Use secant, cosecant and cotangent with their domains, and select the correct squared identities.
lessons.objective: Use secant, cosecant and cotangent with their domains, and select the correct squared identities.
lessons.before: Use this lesson to use secant, cosecant and cotangent with their domains, and select the correct squared identities.
lessons.ideas:
Secant is \(\frac{1}{\cos x}\). Cosecant is \(\frac{1}{\sin x}\). Cotangent is \(\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}\).

Start from \(\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1\). Dividing by cosine squared produces the secant and tangent identity. Dividing by sine squared produces the cosecant and cotangent identity.

After isolating a reciprocal trig function, switch to sine or cosine and find its base angles. Treat a zero cotangent separately.
lessons.method:
Read the familiar sine or cosine coordinate first. Take a reciprocal only after making sure its denominator is not zero. For cotangent, the quotient of the two coordinates works whenever sine is non-zero. You can also take the reciprocal of tangent on their common domain when tangent is non-zero. At the top of the unit circle, cosine is zero and sine is one, so cotangent is zero even though tangent is undefined.

The choice depends on the two squared functions in the question. For a squared secant use \(\sec^2x=1+\tan^2x\). For a squared cosecant use \(\operatorname{{cosec}}^2x=1+\cot^2x\). Dividing by a squared factor still requires that factor to be non-zero. If the question asks for a function value and not its square, choose a sign using information about the quadrant.

Set the denominator values aside before solving. Take the reciprocal of both sides when the isolated function is non-zero. If cotangent alone is zero, its numerator cosine must be zero and sine must be non-zero. Find every possible argument and return to the original angle by checking its bounds.
mistakes: A reciprocal function takes one divided by a trig value. An inverse function returns an angle from a trig value.
Match the related pair before rearranging. A tangent term goes with secant, and a cotangent term goes with cosecant.
Do not take the reciprocal of zero. Check the original domain again after replacing the function.

examples.title: Read an exact trigonometric value
examples.question: Find the exact value of \(\operatorname{cosec}\left(-840^\circ\right)\).
examples.solution:
After removing whole turns, evaluate \(\operatorname{cosec}\left(240^\circ\right)\).

The reference angle is \(60^\circ\). Use the signs of the coordinates in the actual quadrant.

Cosecant has exact value \(- \frac{2 \sqrt{3}}{3}\).

Answer: \(- \frac{2 \sqrt{3}}{3}\).

examples.title: Use an identity to find a squared value
examples.question: It is known that \(u=2190^\circ\) and \(\sin\left(u\right)=\frac{1}{2}\). Find \(\cos^2u\).
examples.solution:
Use \(\cos^2u=1-\sin^2u\).

Square \(\frac{1}{2}\) before substituting it. The square removes any negative sign.

Answer: \(\frac{3}{4}\).

examples.title: Find every solution in the domain
examples.question: Solve \(4\cot\left(x-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=4 \sqrt{3}\) for \(- \frac{2 \pi}{3}\le x\le \frac{7 \pi}{3}\). Give exact answers.
examples.solution:
Subtract the constant and divide by the coefficient to obtain \(\cot\left(u\right)=\sqrt{3}\). Use the reciprocal to solve \(\tan\left(u\right)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\).

The given interval for the full argument \(u=x-\frac{\pi}{4}\) is \(- \frac{11 \pi}{12}\le u\le\frac{25 \pi}{12}\). Solve for \(x\) after listing the possible arguments.

Within a full period, the argument is \(\frac{\pi}{6}\). Repeat by adding or subtracting \(\pi\).

Answer: \(x=- \frac{7 \pi}{12},\quad \frac{5 \pi}{12},\quad \frac{17 \pi}{12}\).

lessons.title: Quadratic and mixed trigonometric equations
lessons.summary: Rewrite mixed trigonometric equations in one function, factor them and include every permitted solution.
lessons.objective: Rewrite mixed trigonometric equations in one function, factor them and include every permitted solution.
lessons.before: Use this lesson to rewrite mixed trigonometric equations in one function, factor them and include every permitted solution.
lessons.ideas:
If \(\sin^2 u=r^2\) for positive \(r\), then the sine can be either \(r\) or \(-r\).

When a question mixes a reciprocal squared with its partner, replace the squared term to obtain a quadratic in one function.

Use the common domain of the original expressions before clearing a trigonometric denominator.
lessons.method:
Isolate the squared function before taking the roots. On a graph, look for crossings at both the upper and the lower horizontal levels. Write the allowed argument interval first, then list upper-level crossings and lower-level crossings separately. Transform every selected angle back to the original variable. If an equation factors, use the zero-product rule and keep the zero value as well.

With \(\sec^2u\) and \(\tan u\), replace the squared secant first. Name the remaining trig value as a variable and factor or solve the quadratic. For each algebraic result, check it lies in the range of that function. For sine or cosine, any algebraic candidate outside minus one to one has no corresponding angle. Keep the original exclusions when a replacement removed a denominator.

When an equation includes both tangent and cotangent, neither the sine nor the cosine can be zero. Then rewriting cotangent as \(\frac1{\tan u}\) allows a multiplication by tangent. After the multiplication, solve the squared equation. Substitute each group into the original expressions to confirm they are defined. Write final answers in the requested unit and include the stipulated endpoints.
mistakes: Squaring removed the sign. A positive square root alone usually leaves missing solutions.
An algebraic root of the substituted equation is a function value. You still need to find every matching angle.
An algebraic operation can remove a visible denominator. Its old excluded values are still excluded.

examples.title: A squared equation has two signs
examples.question: Solve \(2\cos^2\left(\frac{3}{4}x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\frac{3}{2}\) for \(- \frac{3 \pi}{4}\le x< \frac{13 \pi}{4}\). Give exact answers.
examples.solution:
Divide by \(2\) and take both square roots. The function equals \(\pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

The given interval for the full argument \(u=\frac{3}{4}x+\frac{\pi}{4}\) is \(- \frac{5 \pi}{16}\le u<\frac{43 \pi}{16}\). Solve for \(x\) after listing the possible arguments.

Within a full period, the argument is \(\frac{\pi}{6},\ \frac{5 \pi}{6},\ \frac{7 \pi}{6},\ \frac{11 \pi}{6}\). Repeat by adding or subtracting \(2 \pi\).

Answer: \(x=- \frac{5 \pi}{9},\quad - \frac{\pi}{9},\quad \frac{7 \pi}{9},\quad \frac{11 \pi}{9},\quad \frac{19 \pi}{9},\quad \frac{23 \pi}{9}\).

examples.title: Choose one trigonometric unknown
examples.question: Solve \(2\sec^2\left(\frac{3}{4}x-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)-2\tan\left(\frac{3}{4}x-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=2\) for \(- \frac{5 \pi}{6}\le x< \frac{19 \pi}{6}\).
examples.solution:
Replace \(\sec^2u\) with \(1+\tan^2 u\). The constant terms cancel.

Let \(v=\tan u\). The remaining equation is \(2v(v-1)=0\), so the values are \(0,1\).

The given interval for the full argument \(u=\frac{3}{4}x-\frac{\pi}{6}\) is \(- \frac{19 \pi}{24}\le u<\frac{53 \pi}{24}\). Solve for \(x\) after listing the possible arguments.

Within a full period, the argument is \(0,\ \frac{\pi}{4}\). Repeat by adding or subtracting \(\pi\).

Answer: \(x=- \frac{7 \pi}{9},\quad \frac{2 \pi}{9},\quad \frac{5 \pi}{9},\quad \frac{14 \pi}{9},\quad \frac{17 \pi}{9},\quad \frac{26 \pi}{9}\).

examples.title: Relate tangent and cotangent before solving
examples.question: Solve \(8\cot\left(3x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=24\tan\left(3x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\) for \(- \frac{5 \pi}{6}\le x\le 0\).
examples.solution:
Both sine and cosine of the argument must be non-zero, so \(\cot u=\frac{1}{\tan u}\) can be used.

Multiplying by \(\tan u\) gives \(\tan^2u=\frac{1}{3}\). Keep both square roots.

Within a full period, the argument is \(\frac{\pi}{6},\ \frac{5 \pi}{6}\). Repeat by adding or subtracting \(\pi\).

The given interval for the full argument \(u=3x+\frac{\pi}{4}\) is \(- \frac{9 \pi}{4}\le u\le\frac{\pi}{4}\). Solve for \(x\) after listing the possible arguments.

Answer: \(x=- \frac{29 \pi}{36},\quad - \frac{25 \pi}{36},\quad - \frac{17 \pi}{36},\quad - \frac{13 \pi}{36},\quad - \frac{5 \pi}{36},\quad - \frac{\pi}{36}\).

lessons.title: Proving trigonometric relationships
lessons.summary: Prove identities by rewriting one side, using exact algebra and stating where the original expression exists.
lessons.objective: Prove identities by rewriting one side, using exact algebra and stating where the original expression exists.
lessons.before: Use this lesson to prove identities by rewriting one side, using exact algebra and stating where the original expression exists.
lessons.ideas:
Choose the side with more terms, more brackets or more fractions. Rewrite that side one step at a time until it matches the other.

A sum and a difference of the same terms multiply to a difference of squares. Factor out any common coefficient before using a trig identity.

Rewrite in two basic coordinates, combine the numerator first and cancel only a non-zero factor.
lessons.method:
List what the target uses before you start. If it contains sine and cosine, rewrite tangents and reciprocals in terms of those coordinates. If there are squares, check whether the identity \(\sin^2u+\cos^2u=1\) can turn a difference into a single term. Start from an existing side and show equal expressions line by line.

If the squared terms are secant and tangent at the same argument, their difference is one. Cosecant and cotangent give the same result. Use a new letter to name a complicated shared argument. After simplifying, replace the letter with the given argument. Keep the condition that the denominator of the original terms is non-zero.

Start with the allowed values. Turn reciprocal expressions into fractions with sine or cosine denominators. Rewrite an expression subtracted from its reciprocal over a single denominator. Often the new numerator is one minus the square of one coordinate, which switches it to the other coordinate squared. Now write the divisor as a fraction and multiply by its reciprocal. Keep the original restrictions even when all denominators cancel.
mistakes: Testing one angle supports a check but cannot prove an identity for all allowed angles.
The square of a sum is not the sum of squares. Use the difference-of-squares rule only for matching conjugates.
Cancelling a factor can hide its zeros. A simpler final formula does not fill those gaps in the original expression.

examples.title: Recognise a constant trigonometric expression
examples.question: Find the constant value of \(95\left(\sec^2\left(\frac{5}{6}x\right)-\tan^2\left(\frac{5}{6}x\right)\right)\) throughout its domain.
examples.solution:
\(1+\tan^2u=\sec^2u\) holds where \(\cos u\ne0\).

Subtract the squared tangent term. The factor in brackets is one.

Answer: \(95\).

examples.title: Use an identity to find a squared value
examples.question: It is known that \(u=2940^\circ\) and \(\cot\left(u\right)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\). Find \(\operatorname{cosec}^2u\).
examples.solution:
Use \(\operatorname{cosec}^2u=1+\cot^2u\).

Square \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\) before substituting it. The square removes any negative sign.

Answer: \(\frac{4}{3}\).

examples.title: Find the coefficient in a quotient identity
examples.question: The expression \(\frac{7\operatorname{cosec}\left(\frac{3}{8}x+\pi\right)-7\sin\left(\frac{3}{8}x+\pi\right)}{\cot\left(\frac{3}{8}x+\pi\right)}\) simplifies to \(k\cos\left(\frac{3}{8}x+\pi\right)\) on its domain. Find \(k\).
examples.solution:
Write the reciprocal in terms of sine or cosine. The numerator becomes \(\frac{7(1-\sin^2\left(\frac{3}{8}x+\pi\right))}{\sin\left(\frac{3}{8}x+\pi\right)}\).

The Pythagorean identity gives \(\frac{7\cos^2\left(\frac{3}{8}x+\pi\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{3}{8}x+\pi\right)}\).

Write \(\cot\left(\frac{3}{8}x+\pi\right)\) as \(\frac{\cos\left(\frac{3}{8}x+\pi\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{3}{8}x+\pi\right)}\) and cancel the common factors.

Both the original reciprocal and the divisor must be defined. The divisor also cannot be zero.

Answer: \(7\).

1. The graph is \(y=\tan\left(x\right)\). Find its exact ordinate at \(x=-210^\circ\).

    [2]

  2. Find all x-intercepts of \(y=7\cos\left(\frac{1}{3}x\right)\) for \(-540^\circ\le x\le 1080^\circ\). Give the x-coordinates.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Move along the horizontal axis to the given angle. The repeat distance is \(180^\circ\).

Reducing the input to one cycle gives the ordinate \(- \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\).

Answer: \(- \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\).

(b)

A non-zero scale \(7\) leaves the zeros unchanged.

Within a full period, the argument is \(90^\circ,\ 270^\circ\). Repeat by adding or subtracting \(360^\circ\).

The given interval for the full argument \(u=\frac{1}{3}x\) is \(-180^\circ\le u\le360^\circ\). Solve for \(x\) after listing the possible arguments.

Answer: \(x=-270^\circ,\quad 270^\circ,\quad 810^\circ\).
questions.hint_html:
(a) Start with the angle and read up or down to the curve.

(b) Set the y-value to zero and solve for the angle inside the function.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the period and reference angle to find the y-value.
Find the zeros of the underlying function, repeat across the interval and then undo the angle multiplier.
A non-zero scale \(7\) leaves the zeros unchanged.
\(x=-270^\circ,\quad 270^\circ,\quad 810^\circ\)

questions.title: Compare period and vertical asymptotes
questions.prompt_html:
1. Find the period of the graph \(y=3\tan\left(4x\right)-3\) in degrees.

    [2]

  2. Give the x-coordinates of all vertical asymptotes of \(y=8\tan\left(\frac{3}{4}x\right)+1\) for \(- \frac{4 \pi}{3}\le x\le \frac{8 \pi}{3}\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

One full repeat of tangent takes \(180^\circ\) in the argument.

The input multiplier is \(4\). Divide the original period by \(4\).

Answer: \(45^\circ\).

(b)

The graph is undefined where the cosine of the argument is zero.

Within a full period, the argument is \(\frac{\pi}{2}\). Repeat by adding or subtracting \(\pi\).

The given interval for the full argument \(u=\frac{3}{4}x\) is \(- \pi\le u\le2 \pi\). Solve for \(x\) after listing the possible arguments.

Answer: \(x=- \frac{2 \pi}{3},\quad \frac{2 \pi}{3},\quad 2 \pi\).
questions.hint_html:
(a) Find how much the argument must change for one full repeat. Divide by its input multiplier.

(b) Find where the cosine in the denominator vanishes. The vertical shift does not alter these x-coordinates.

marking_criteria.description_html: Divide the basic period of the stated trigonometric function by the input scale.
Solve for the odd multiples of a quarter-turn in the argument and keep the right interval.
The graph is undefined where the cosine of the argument is zero.
\(x=- \frac{2 \pi}{3},\quad \frac{2 \pi}{3},\quad 2 \pi\)

1. Give the x-coordinates of all vertical asymptotes of \(y=6\tan\left(\frac{3}{4}x\right)-2\) for \(0\le x\le \frac{8 \pi}{3}\).

    [3]

  2. Sketch \(y=6\tan\left(\frac{3}{4}x\right)-2\) for \(0\le x\le \frac{8 \pi}{3}\). Include all asymptotes.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(x=\frac{2 \pi}{3},\quad 2 \pi\)

(b) Sketch through \(\left(0,-2\right),\ \left(\frac{\pi}{3},4\right),\ \left(\pi,-8\right),\ \left(\frac{4 \pi}{3},-2\right),\ \left(\frac{5 \pi}{3},4\right),\ \left(\frac{7 \pi}{3},-8\right),\ \left(\frac{8 \pi}{3},-2\right)\). Draw and label asymptotes at \(x=\frac{2 \pi}{3},\ 2 \pi\). Join the landmarks with the expected smooth curves. Draw each branch separately on its own side of an asymptote.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The graph is undefined where the cosine of the argument is zero.

Within a full period, the argument is \(\frac{\pi}{2}\). Repeat by adding or subtracting \(\pi\).

The given interval for the full argument \(u=\frac{3}{4}x\) is \(0\le u\le2 \pi\). Solve for \(x\) after listing the possible arguments.

Answer: \(x=\frac{2 \pi}{3},\quad 2 \pi\).

(b)

The unreflected curve repeats after \(\frac{4 \pi}{3}\) and its vertical shift is \(-2\).

Use the following sketch points: \(\left(0,-2\right),\ \left(\frac{\pi}{3},4\right),\ \left(\pi,-8\right),\ \left(\frac{4 \pi}{3},-2\right),\ \left(\frac{5 \pi}{3},4\right),\ \left(\frac{7 \pi}{3},-8\right),\ \left(\frac{8 \pi}{3},-2\right)\).

Draw and label asymptotes at \(x=\frac{2 \pi}{3},\ 2 \pi\). Tangent is unbounded along its asymptotes. Join the landmarks with the expected smooth curves. Draw each branch separately on its own side of an asymptote.

Answer: Sketch through \(\left(0,-2\right),\ \left(\frac{\pi}{3},4\right),\ \left(\pi,-8\right),\ \left(\frac{4 \pi}{3},-2\right),\ \left(\frac{5 \pi}{3},4\right),\ \left(\frac{7 \pi}{3},-8\right),\ \left(\frac{8 \pi}{3},-2\right)\). Draw and label asymptotes at \(x=\frac{2 \pi}{3},\ 2 \pi\). Join the landmarks with the expected smooth curves. Draw each branch separately on its own side of an asymptote..

(a) Find where the cosine in the denominator vanishes. The vertical shift does not alter these x-coordinates.

One full repeat of tangent takes \(180^\circ\) in the argument.

The input multiplier is \(4\). Divide the original period by \(4\).

(b) Apply the modulus after evaluating the scaled and shifted trigonometric expression.

1. Solve \(4\sec^2\left(x-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)-4\tan\left(x-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=4\) for \(- \frac{\pi}{12}\le x< \frac{35 \pi}{12}\).

    [4]

  2. Solve \(3\operatorname{cosec}^2\left(2x\right)=4\) for \(-30^\circ\le x< 150^\circ\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Replace \(\sec^2u\) with \(1+\tan^2 u\). The constant terms cancel.

Let \(v=\tan u\). The remaining equation is \(4v(v-1)=0\), so the values are \(0,1\).

The given interval for the full argument \(u=x-\frac{\pi}{4}\) is \(- \frac{\pi}{3}\le u<\frac{8 \pi}{3}\). Solve for \(x\) after listing the possible arguments.

Within a full period, the argument is \(0,\ \frac{\pi}{4}\). Repeat by adding or subtracting \(\pi\).

Answer: \(x=\frac{\pi}{4},\quad \frac{\pi}{2},\quad \frac{5 \pi}{4},\quad \frac{3 \pi}{2},\quad \frac{9 \pi}{4},\quad \frac{5 \pi}{2}\).

(b)

Use \(\operatorname{cosec}^2u=1+\cot^2u\).

Rearranging gives \(\cot^2u=\frac{1}{3}\). Keep both signs for the function.

The given interval for the full argument \(u=2x\) is \(-60^\circ\le u<300^\circ\). Solve for \(x\) after listing the possible arguments.

Within a full period, the argument is \(60^\circ,\ 120^\circ\). Repeat by adding or subtracting \(180^\circ\).

Answer: \(x=-30^\circ,\quad 30^\circ,\quad 60^\circ,\quad 120^\circ\).
questions.hint_html:
(a) Convert both terms to the same function. Keep the factor that gives a zero tangent.

(b) Use the reciprocal Pythagorean identity. Check both signs of the resulting basic trigonometric value.

Within a full period, the argument is \(\frac{\pi}{4},\ \frac{3 \pi}{4}\). Repeat by adding or subtracting \(\pi\).

The given interval for the full argument \(u=x-\frac{\pi}{12}\) is \(- \frac{\pi}{4}\le u\le\frac{11 \pi}{4}\). Solve for \(x\) after listing the possible arguments.

1. Prove that \((8\operatorname{cosec}\left(2x+\frac{\pi}{12}\right)+8\cot\left(2x+\frac{\pi}{12}\right))(8\operatorname{cosec}\left(2x+\frac{\pi}{12}\right)-8\cot\left(2x+\frac{\pi}{12}\right))\equiv 64\) wherever the left-hand side is defined. State the restriction on the argument.

    [4]

  2. For which values of \(x\) is \(\cot\left(2x+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\) undefined on \(- \frac{\pi}{4}\le x< \frac{3 \pi}{4}\)?

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Multiply the conjugate brackets using the difference of two squares.

Factor out \(64\). The remaining difference is one by the cosecant and cotangent identity.

Both terms in the original brackets have denominator \(\sin\left(2x+\frac{\pi}{12}\right)\). Exclude its zeros.

Answer: The product equals \(64\), provided \(\sin\left(2x+\frac{\pi}{12}\right)\ne0\)..

(b)

The denominator of this expression is \(\sin u\).

The given interval for the full argument \(u=2x+\frac{\pi}{6}\) is \(- \frac{\pi}{3}\le u<\frac{5 \pi}{3}\). Solve for \(x\) after listing the possible arguments.

Within a full period, the argument is \(0\). Repeat by adding or subtracting \(\pi\).

Answer: \(x=- \frac{\pi}{12},\quad \frac{5 \pi}{12}\).
questions.hint_html:
(a) Name the repeated argument u. Expand the two conjugate brackets before choosing an identity.

(b) Write the reciprocal or quotient as a fraction. Set the denominator equal to zero.

State the exclusion from the denominator of the original expression.
The product equals \(64\), provided \(\sin\left(2x+\frac{\pi}{12}\right)\ne0\).
Identify zeros of the denominator and map them from the argument interval to the x-interval.
The denominator of this expression is \(\sin u\).

questions.title: Prove a quotient relationship with cancellations
questions.prompt_html:
1. Prove that \(\frac{7\sec\left(\frac{5}{6}x+15^\circ\right)-7\cos\left(\frac{5}{6}x+15^\circ\right)}{\tan\left(\frac{5}{6}x+15^\circ\right)}\equiv 7\sin\left(\frac{5}{6}x+15^\circ\right)\). State any restrictions on the sine and cosine of the argument.

    [5]

  2. Find the constant value of \(\frac{\sec^2\left(\frac{1}{2}x\right)-\tan^2\left(\frac{1}{2}x\right)}{29}+\frac{3}{2}\left(\sin^2\left(\frac{1}{2}x\right)+\cos^2\left(\frac{1}{2}x\right)\right)\) throughout its domain.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a) The expression is \(7\sin\left(\frac{5}{6}x+15^\circ\right)\) when both \(\sin\left(\frac{5}{6}x+15^\circ\right)\) and \(\cos\left(\frac{5}{6}x+15^\circ\right)\) are non-zero.

(b) \(\frac{89}{58}\)
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Write the reciprocal in terms of sine or cosine. The numerator becomes \(\frac{7(1-\cos^2\left(\frac{5}{6}x+15^\circ\right))}{\cos\left(\frac{5}{6}x+15^\circ\right)}\).

The Pythagorean identity gives \(\frac{7\sin^2\left(\frac{5}{6}x+15^\circ\right)}{\cos\left(\frac{5}{6}x+15^\circ\right)}\).

Write \(\tan\left(\frac{5}{6}x+15^\circ\right)\) as \(\frac{\sin\left(\frac{5}{6}x+15^\circ\right)}{\cos\left(\frac{5}{6}x+15^\circ\right)}\) and cancel the common factors.

Both the original reciprocal and the divisor must be defined. The divisor also cannot be zero.

Answer: The expression is \(7\sin\left(\frac{5}{6}x+15^\circ\right)\) when both \(\sin\left(\frac{5}{6}x+15^\circ\right)\) and \(\cos\left(\frac{5}{6}x+15^\circ\right)\) are non-zero..

(b)

Use \(\sec^2u-\tan^2u=1\) to simplify the numerator.

Use \(\sin^2u+\cos^2u=1\) to simplify the product.

The final value is \(\frac{1}{29}+\frac{3}{2}=\frac{89}{58}\).

Answer: \(\frac{89}{58}\).

(a) Begin with the side containing the quotient. Rewrite the numerator and the divisor before cancelling.

(b) Treat the numerator and the second pair as two different Pythagorean identities.

The Pythagorean identity gives \(\frac{7\sin^2\left(\frac{5}{6}x+15^\circ\right)}{\cos\left(\frac{5}{6}x+15^\circ\right)}\).

1. Prove that \((8\operatorname{cosec}\left(2x+\frac{\pi}{12}\right)+8\cot\left(2x+\frac{\pi}{12}\right))(8\operatorname{cosec}\left(2x+\frac{\pi}{12}\right)-8\cot\left(2x+\frac{\pi}{12}\right))\equiv 64\) wherever the left-hand side is defined. State the restriction on the argument.

    [4]

  2. Prove that \(\frac{5\operatorname{cosec}\left(\frac{3}{8}x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)-5\sin\left(\frac{3}{8}x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)}{\cot\left(\frac{3}{8}x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)}\equiv 5\cos\left(\frac{3}{8}x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\). State any restrictions on the sine and cosine of the argument.

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a) The product equals \(64\), provided \(\sin\left(2x+\frac{\pi}{12}\right)\ne0\).

(b) The expression is \(5\cos\left(\frac{3}{8}x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\) when both \(\sin\left(\frac{3}{8}x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\) and \(\cos\left(\frac{3}{8}x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\) are non-zero.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Multiply the conjugate brackets using the difference of two squares.

Factor out \(64\). The remaining difference is one by the cosecant and cotangent identity.

Both terms in the original brackets have denominator \(\sin\left(2x+\frac{\pi}{12}\right)\). Exclude its zeros.

Answer: The product equals \(64\), provided \(\sin\left(2x+\frac{\pi}{12}\right)\ne0\)..

(b)

Write the reciprocal in terms of sine or cosine. The numerator becomes \(\frac{5(1-\sin^2\left(\frac{3}{8}x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right))}{\sin\left(\frac{3}{8}x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)}\).

The Pythagorean identity gives \(\frac{5\cos^2\left(\frac{3}{8}x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{3}{8}x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)}\).

Write \(\cot\left(\frac{3}{8}x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\) as \(\frac{\cos\left(\frac{3}{8}x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{3}{8}x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)}\) and cancel the common factors.

Both the original reciprocal and the divisor must be defined. The divisor also cannot be zero.

Answer: The expression is \(5\cos\left(\frac{3}{8}x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\) when both \(\sin\left(\frac{3}{8}x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\) and \(\cos\left(\frac{3}{8}x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\) are non-zero..
questions.hint_html:
(a) Name the repeated argument u. Expand the two conjugate brackets before choosing an identity.

(b) Begin with the side containing the quotient. Rewrite the numerator and the divisor before cancelling.

questions.title: Prove a conjugate relationship and justify its domain
questions.prompt_html:
1. Prove that \((9\sec\left(3x+15^\circ\right)+9\tan\left(3x+15^\circ\right))(9\sec\left(3x+15^\circ\right)-9\tan\left(3x+15^\circ\right))\equiv 81\) wherever the left-hand side is defined. State the restriction on the argument.

    [4]

  2. For which values of \(x\) is \(\sec\left(\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{\pi}{12}\right)\) undefined on \(- \frac{\pi}{3}\le x< \frac{43 \pi}{6}\)?

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Multiply the conjugate brackets using the difference of two squares.

Factor out \(81\). The remaining difference is one by the secant and tangent identity.

Both terms in the original brackets have denominator \(\cos\left(3x+15^\circ\right)\). Exclude its zeros.

Answer: The product equals \(81\), provided \(\cos\left(3x+15^\circ\right)\ne0\)..

(b)

The denominator of this expression is \(\cos u\).

The given interval for the full argument \(u=\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{\pi}{12}\) is \(- \frac{7 \pi}{36}\le u<\frac{83 \pi}{36}\). Solve for \(x\) after listing the possible arguments.

Within a full period, the argument is \(\frac{\pi}{2}\). Repeat by adding or subtracting \(\pi\).

Answer: \(x=\frac{7 \pi}{4},\quad \frac{19 \pi}{4}\).
questions.hint_html:
(a) Name the repeated argument u. Expand the two conjugate brackets before choosing an identity.

(b) Write the reciprocal or quotient as a fraction. Set the denominator equal to zero.

questions.title: Prove a quotient relationship with cancellations
questions.prompt_html:
1. Prove that \(\frac{4\sec\left(3x+30^\circ\right)-4\cos\left(3x+30^\circ\right)}{\tan\left(3x+30^\circ\right)}\equiv 4\sin\left(3x+30^\circ\right)\). State any restrictions on the sine and cosine of the argument.

    [5]

  2. Find the constant value of \(\frac{\sec^2\left(3x\right)-\tan^2\left(3x\right)}{36}+\frac{5}{2}\left(\sin^2\left(3x\right)+\cos^2\left(3x\right)\right)\) throughout its domain.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a) The expression is \(4\sin\left(3x+30^\circ\right)\) when both \(\sin\left(3x+30^\circ\right)\) and \(\cos\left(3x+30^\circ\right)\) are non-zero.

(b) \(\frac{91}{36}\)
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Write the reciprocal in terms of sine or cosine. The numerator becomes \(\frac{4(1-\cos^2\left(3x+30^\circ\right))}{\cos\left(3x+30^\circ\right)}\).

The Pythagorean identity gives \(\frac{4\sin^2\left(3x+30^\circ\right)}{\cos\left(3x+30^\circ\right)}\).

Write \(\tan\left(3x+30^\circ\right)\) as \(\frac{\sin\left(3x+30^\circ\right)}{\cos\left(3x+30^\circ\right)}\) and cancel the common factors.

Both the original reciprocal and the divisor must be defined. The divisor also cannot be zero.

Answer: The expression is \(4\sin\left(3x+30^\circ\right)\) when both \(\sin\left(3x+30^\circ\right)\) and \(\cos\left(3x+30^\circ\right)\) are non-zero..

(b)

Use \(\sec^2u-\tan^2u=1\) to simplify the numerator.

Use \(\sin^2u+\cos^2u=1\) to simplify the product.

The final value is \(\frac{1}{36}+\frac{5}{2}=\frac{91}{36}\).

Answer: \(\frac{91}{36}\).
questions.hint_html:
(a) Begin with the side containing the quotient. Rewrite the numerator and the divisor before cancelling.

(b) Treat the numerator and the second pair as two different Pythagorean identities.

marking_criteria.description_html: Express the numerator as a fraction with one trigonometric denominator.

The Pythagorean identity gives \(\frac{4\sin^2\left(3x+30^\circ\right)}{\cos\left(3x+30^\circ\right)}\).
Keep both original denominator restrictions after simplifying.
The expression is \(4\sin\left(3x+30^\circ\right)\) when both \(\sin\left(3x+30^\circ\right)\) and \(\cos\left(3x+30^\circ\right)\) are non-zero.
Apply both Pythagorean identities and combine the resulting constants.
Use \(\sec^2u-\tan^2u=1\) to simplify the numerator.

questions.title: Prove a conjugate relationship and justify its domain
questions.prompt_html:
1. Prove that \((10\sec\left(4x+30^\circ\right)+10\tan\left(4x+30^\circ\right))(10\sec\left(4x+30^\circ\right)-10\tan\left(4x+30^\circ\right))\equiv 100\) wherever the left-hand side is defined. State the restriction on the argument.

    [4]

  2. For which values of \(x\) is \(\operatorname{cosec}\left(4x+\frac{\pi}{12}\right)\) undefined on \(- \frac{5 \pi}{12}\le x< \frac{\pi}{3}\)?

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Multiply the conjugate brackets using the difference of two squares.

Factor out \(100\). The remaining difference is one by the secant and tangent identity.

Both terms in the original brackets have denominator \(\cos\left(4x+30^\circ\right)\). Exclude its zeros.

Answer: The product equals \(100\), provided \(\cos\left(4x+30^\circ\right)\ne0\)..

(b)

The denominator of this expression is \(\sin u\).

The given interval for the full argument \(u=4x+\frac{\pi}{12}\) is \(- \frac{19 \pi}{12}\le u<\frac{17 \pi}{12}\). Solve for \(x\) after listing the possible arguments.

Within a full period, the argument is \(0\). Repeat by adding or subtracting \(\pi\).

Answer: \(x=- \frac{13 \pi}{48},\quad - \frac{\pi}{48},\quad \frac{11 \pi}{48}\).

questions.title: Prove a conjugate relationship and justify its domain
questions.prompt_html:
1. Prove that \((2\operatorname{cosec}\left(\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)+2\cot\left(\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right))(2\operatorname{cosec}\left(\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)-2\cot\left(\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right))\equiv 4\) wherever the left-hand side is defined. State the restriction on the argument.

    [4]

  2. For which values of \(x\) is \(\cot\left(\frac{1}{2}x+30^\circ\right)\) undefined on \(-90^\circ\le x< 630^\circ\)?

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Multiply the conjugate brackets using the difference of two squares.

Factor out \(4\). The remaining difference is one by the cosecant and cotangent identity.

Both terms in the original brackets have denominator \(\sin\left(\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\). Exclude its zeros.

Answer: The product equals \(4\), provided \(\sin\left(\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\ne0\)..

(b)

The denominator of this expression is \(\sin u\).

The given interval for the full argument \(u=\frac{1}{2}x+30^\circ\) is \(-15^\circ\le u<345^\circ\). Solve for \(x\) after listing the possible arguments.

Within a full period, the argument is \(0\). Repeat by adding or subtracting \(180^\circ\).

Answer: \(x=-60^\circ,\quad 300^\circ\).
